definition: The form a substance has: solid, liquid or gas. The same substance can exist in all three forms, depending on the temperature.
A model in which substances are drawn as small balls, particles. The particles are always moving, and the higher the temperature, the faster they move.
A fourth form of matter where the gas is so hot that electrons have been torn loose from the atoms. Plasma is found in lightning, the northern lights and in the Sun.
The change from solid form to liquid form when the substance is heated, for example when ice becomes water.
The change from liquid form to solid form when the substance is cooled, for example when water freezes into ice.
The temperature at which a pure substance melts (and solidifies). For water it is 0 °C.
When particles leave the surface of a liquid and become gas. It happens at all temperatures, but faster when it is warm, dry and windy.
When a liquid becomes gas throughout the whole liquid, so that bubbles form. It happens at the substance's boiling point.
The temperature at which a liquid boils. For water it is 100 °C at normal air pressure.
The change from gas to liquid when the gas is cooled, for example when water vapour turns into droplets on a cold glass.
The change directly from solid form to gas without the substance becoming liquid, for example when dry ice becomes carbon dioxide gas.
A change in which no new substances are formed. The substance is the same afterwards, just in a different form or mixed with something else.
A substance that contains only one kind of particle, either an element or a chemical compound. It has definite melting and boiling points.
How much mass a substance has per volume, ρ = m / V, often in g/cm³. Substances with a higher density than the liquid sink in it.
Two or more substances that are together without having reacted with each other. Each substance keeps its properties.
A mixture that looks the same everywhere, so that you cannot see the different parts, for example salt water and air.
A mixture where you can see that it consists of different parts, for example sand in water or granite.
A homogeneous mixture where one substance is spread out as very small particles in another, for example salt in water.
A mixture where solid grains are suspended in a liquid, for example clay in water. The grains sink over time.
A mixture where small droplets of a liquid are suspended in another liquid that they do not dissolve in, for example oil in water or milk.
A substance that stops an emulsion from separating, for example egg yolk in mayonnaise.
A mixture of metals (or a metal with a little of another element), for example bronze, brass and steel.
The substance that dissolves something else in a solution, for example the water in salt water.
The substance that has been dissolved in a solution, for example the salt in salt water.
A solution that cannot dissolve any more of the substance. If you add more, it lies undissolved at the bottom.
How much of a substance can be dissolved in a certain solvent at a certain temperature.
A way of dividing a mixture into its parts. The method makes use of the fact that the substances differ in some property.
Letting a mixture pass through a sieve with holes of a certain size, so that small parts go through and large ones stay behind.
Letting a suspension stand still so that the heavier grains sink and collect at the bottom.
The deposit at the bottom: the grains that have sunk to the bottom when a suspension has been left to stand.
Carefully pouring off the liquid from a sediment so that the deposit at the bottom stays behind.
Pouring a mixture through a filter with very small holes. The liquid goes through, the undissolved grains stay behind.
The liquid that has passed through the filter.
Spinning a mixture very fast so that the heavier parts are pressed outwards and end up at the bottom of the tube.
Letting the solvent evaporate or boil away so that the dissolved substance remains as a solid.
Heating a mixture so that the substance with the lowest boiling point becomes vapour, which is then cooled and becomes liquid again in a condenser.
The liquid that is collected when the vapour has been cooled and condensed in a distillation.
Using a solvent to dissolve out what you want from a solid mixture, for example flavour from tea leaves.
A method for separating and identifying substances in a mixture because they travel at different speeds, for example on filter paper.
The distance a substance has travelled divided by the distance the solvent has travelled in chromatography. The value is between 0 and 1.
When two solutions are mixed and a new, insoluble solid substance forms that sinks to the bottom. The substance is also called a precipitate.
Finding out what a substance is or what a sample contains (detecting), and how much it contains (measuring).
A measure of how acidic or basic something is, on a scale from about 0 to 14. pH 7 is neutral.
A substance that changes colour depending on whether the solution is acidic or basic, for example pH paper.
A plant that cleans wastewater in several steps, including screens, sedimentation, bacteria and precipitation, before the water is released.
A method where water is pressed through a very dense membrane that stops the dissolved salt. It is used to remove salt from seawater.
A guess that is based on what you already know and that can be tested through an investigation.

Something that can be changed or measured in an investigation. The one you change is the independent variable, the one you measure is the dependent variable, and everything else must be kept the same (constant).
Something that may have made a measurement result less reliable, for example a poor measurement, different conditions between experiments or a broken piece of equipment.
